scenes.name: Rapcore y New Metal
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Body Count, el grupo del rapero Ice-T, abre el rapcore con temas atractivos para chicos de todas las razas; a finales de la década las voces rapeadas se ponen de moda, aunque pocos de esos grupos son metal. Spin dedica en agosto de 1998 un reportaje al «New Metal» (Korn, Limp Bizkit con su DJ fijo), un híbrido que bebe tanto del rock alternativo, el hip-hop y el hardcore del skate californiano como de Black Sabbath y Slayer, y Rolling Stone lleva en febrero de 1999 a Rob Zombie en portada con los «10 mejores grupos de metal». Weinstein se pregunta por qué se llama metal a lo que sus músicos no quieren que se llame así: la etiqueta da una imagen más blanca y más rock, y su uso promiscuo es a la vez prueba y causa del regreso del metal. ¿Es metal Rage Against the Machine? ¿Y Sevendust o Limp Bizkit?

podcast.title: Participant in 1997 Tour
podcast.body: Limp Bizkit was among the various bands participating in the Warped Tour in 1997. "Some band called Limp Biscuit was there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inciting Violence at Woodstock 99 (1999)
podcast.body: Limp Bizkit performed at Woodstock 99, a festival that descended into widespread violence and chaos. The band, specifically, was attributed with inciting some of the violence when they played their song "Break Stuff" on the Saturday night of the festival, contributing to the escalating frustration and hatred among the 200,000 attendees. "the mob began to take over, probably starting on the Saturday night, when Limpiske played their song, Break Stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Woodstock 1999 Crowd Incitement
podcast.body: Limp Bizkit was present at Woodstock 1999, where their performance was associated with encouraging the crowd to engage in frenzied, uncontrolled behavior. This contributed to the overall violence and issues at the festival. "Lim Biscuit, who was also Woodstock 99, encouraging the crowd to go nuts..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 2000 Sales Performance
podcast.body: The band sold 4 million records in the year 2000, making them one of the few successful New Metal acts during a time when rock music was struggling. "Limp Biscuit sold 4 million records in 2000."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Big Day Out Tragedy and Lawsuits (2001)
podcast.body: As headliners at the Big Day Out festival in Sydney on January 21, 2001, Limp Bizkit's singer Fred Durst had pre-show concerns about inadequate security barriers, which he discussed multiple times with the promoter. Despite assurances, a massive crush occurred towards the stage during their first song, resulting in approximately 30 injuries and the death of 15-year-old Jessica Milicic, who died five days later from a heart attack caused by asphyxiation. An investigation closed in November 2002 without charges, but new security rules were implemented. Milicic's parents filed a civil suit against Limp Bizkit in November 2004, and the band was also sued by their own insurance company over legal fees, leading to speculation that these events contributed to their subsequent quiet period. "So, is it any wonder we haven't heard anything from Limpbiscat since then?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Guitarist Wes Borland's Departures and Return (2001-2004)
podcast.body: Guitarist Wes Borland initially quit the band in 2001. He was replaced by Mike Smith, but Smith departed by 2004, leading to Borland's return. "First guitarist Wes Borland had quit 2001. He was replaced by Mike Smith, but by 2004 he had gone. Wes was back."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Jessica Michalik's Death at Big Day Out (2001)
podcast.body: At the Big Day Out Festival in Australia in 2001, 16-year-old Jessica Michalik was crushed in the mosh pit during Limp Bizkit's performance, dying five days later from a heart attack related to asphyxiation. The coroner criticized singer Fred Durst for "alarming and inflammatory comments" made as EMS tried to rescue Michalik. "16-year-old Jessica Malachik was crushed in the pit and died of a heart attack related to a sixiation five days later."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Breakup Date (November 8, 2005)
podcast.body: This date, following the release of their greatest hits album and subsequent silence, is used as the band's official breakup date. "So what we're going to do is use that date as our breakup date. November 8th 2005."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Public Disfavor & Internal Issues (Mid-2005)
podcast.body: By mid-2005, Limp Biscuit, and Fred Durst in particular, had "worn out their welcome with the public" as their sound and approach had gone "out of style." This period was also marked by internal problems. "But by the middle of 2005, Limp Biscuit in general and Fred Durst in particular had worn out their welcome with the public."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Reunion Rumors (Fall 2008)
podcast.body: By the fall of 2008, rumors began circulating that the band's internal differences had been resolved and they were reuniting. "There were rumors that differences had been fixed and that Limp Biscuit was back together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: First Reunion Gig (May 2009) – Riga, Latvia
podcast.body: Three months after the reunion announcement, the original lineup, which had not been seen together in eight years, played their first gig in Riga, Latvia. "Three months later, the original lineup, something that we hadn't seen in eight years played their first gig together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: New Album Work Begins (August 24, 2009)
podcast.body: By August 24, 2009, all members of the reunited band had begun working on a new album. "And in August the 24th of 2009, everyone started working on a new album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Reunion Announcement (February 11, 2009)
podcast.body: On this date, Fred Durst posted a message on Twitter – "1am Pacific time. Limp Biscuit.com tonight" – signaling the band's official return. "And on February 11th of 2009, those who were following Fred on Twitter... got this message. 1am Pacific time. Limp Biscuit.com tonight."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Big Day Out Festival Crowd Crush (Sydney, Australia)
podcast.body: During Limp Bizkit's performance at the Big Day Out Festival in Sydney, Australia, a massive mosh pit formed in front of the stage, leading to the crushing of a woman named Jessica Mitchellick. She was rescued and transported to a hospital but tragically died five days later from a heart attack. "Let Biscuit found themselves in a bad situation at the Big Day Out Festival in Sydney, Australia."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: California New Punk Scene
podcast.body: Limp Bizkit is mentioned as a band that emerged years later from the "new punk" bases being laid in California in the late 1980s. "saldrían pues... Limp Bizkit."

srcs.episode: Cuál fue el primer disco de Grunge?

podcast.title: Discovery by Korn's Fieldy
podcast.body: After Korn's encounter with Fred Durst, Durst strategically sent a Limp Bizkit demo tape to Fieldy, a member of Korn. Fieldy was impressed by the demo and subsequently passed it on to Korn's management and the emerging nu-metal producer Ross Robinson. This crucial step paved the way for Limp Bizkit's major label deal. "When Corn got home, Fieldy found a limp biscuit demo in his mailbox."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 3

podcast.title: Drummer John Otto's Issues
podcast.body: Drummer John Otto also experienced issues that limited his participation. "And drummer John Otto had issues too. So he wasn't able to do much."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fred Durst as Executive
podcast.body: Executives at the band's record company thought highly enough of Fred Durst to appoint him an executive. "executives at their record company thought enough of Fred Durst to make him an executive."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Fred Durst's Career as Interscope Records Executive
podcast.body: Following his success with Limp Bizkit, Fred Durst transitioned into a significant role as a major executive at Interscope Records. This career path was a direct result of the opportunities that arose from his initial connection with Korn. "Fred has since become a major executive at Interscope Records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 3

podcast.title: Fred Durst's Role in Crowd Incitement
podcast.body: Limp Bizkit's vocalist, Fred Durst, was specifically cited for intensely riling up the crowd, contributing to an atmosphere where a negative incident, such as the fatal crowd crush at Big Day Out, was almost inevitable. Although initial lawsuits were dismissed, an insurance company later sued the band in 2005, arguing that Durst had incited the crowd to rush the stage. "At the same time, Lent Biscuit, vocalist Fred Durst especially, riled up the crowd so much that something bad was almost an inevitability."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence from Body Count
podcast.body: Limp Bizkit can be linked in a direct line of influence back to Body Count, indicating Body Count's role in the nu-metal movement. "So basically, you can draw a line from Body Count, right through corn, slipknot, and limp biscuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence from Living Color
podcast.body: Limp Bizkit was one of the bands inspired by Living Color's musical style. "another band that inspired groups like Rage Against the Machine, and Limbiscuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lawsuits Following Michalik's Death
podcast.body: Jessica Michalik's parents filed a civil suit against Limp Bizkit after her death. Subsequently, Limp Bizkit was also sued by their own insurance company, which argued that their policy did not cover lawsuits arising from such incidents, highlighting the increasing financial and legal risks associated with moshing. "Her parents filed a civil suit against Lim Biscuit. The band was then sued by their own insurance company, saying that these kinds of lawsuits weren't covered by their policy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Major Label Deal and Rise to Prominence
podcast.body: Following the positive reception of their demo by Korn's Fieldy and producer Ross Robinson, Limp Bizkit quickly secured a major label deal. This set them on a path to become one of the most successful and impactful bands of the nu-metal era, known for their aggressive and in-your-face style. "And before long, limp biscuit had a major label deal and were on their way to becoming one of the most successful and most in-your-face bands of the new metal era."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 3

podcast.title: Promoter Liability for Crowd Control
podcast.body: An investigation conducted by the state coroner into the death of Jessica Mitchellick at the Big Day Out Festival concluded that the promoters were legally liable for failing to adequately police the crowd density in front of the stage during Limp Bizkit's set. "an investigation by the state corner found that the promoters were, in fact, libel for not policing the crowd density in front of the stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rapid Decline
podcast.body: The band experienced a swift decline at the end of the 90s due to "ill-advised career moves," including their controversial Woodstock 99 appearance, and the release of "below-par albums." "they flamed up pretty fast at the end of the 90s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Symbol of New Metal's Downfall
podcast.body: Limp Biscuit came to symbolize "the worst of new metal" and became the central focus of the backlash against the genre, despite attracting 50,000 people to stadium shows. "If it's just one band that came to symbolize the worst of new metal and a group that was the focus of the backlash, it was Limp Biscuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Time Apart (3 years, 3 months, 3 days)
podcast.body: The band was apart for this duration, from their designated breakup date of November 8, 2005, to their reunion announcement on February 11, 2009. "Let Biscuit and Nookie, apart for three years, three months and three days."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Woodstock '99 Violence
podcast.body: Limp Bizkit's performance at the 30th-anniversary Woodstock Festival in Rome, New York, in the summer of 1999 was marred by significant violence, sexual assaults, and vandalism, which cast a negative light on both the band and the new metal scene. "Later that summer, they played the 30th anniversary Woodstock Festival in Rome, New York. And their set was marred by violence, sexual assaults, and vandalism."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 1: The Sad State of Rock

podcast.title: Zero DB Initiative Signatory
podcast.body: Limp Bizkit is among the artists who signed the Zero DB initiative, which was formed in 2008 as part of the charity Reprieve. This group encourages the condemnation of music as torture and advocates for governments to enforce international treaties related to prisoner treatment. "The Sinees include Tom Morello, average against the machine, members of REM, rise against Pearl Jam, Trent Reznor, Limp Biscuit, system of a down, disturbed the estate of Prince, the Chili Peppers, Eminem, Marilyn Manson, Neil Diamond, Dr. Dre, and a host of others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

concerts.title: Woodstock 99 Appearance
concerts.body: The band's appearance at Woodstock 99 was marred by violence and destruction, contributing to their "ill-advised career moves" and backlash. "an appearance at Woodstock 99 that was marred by violence and destruction."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Assorted Controversial Actions
xref.body: Al Jourgensen has a long history of controversial and confrontational behaviors, including stealing drugs from Courtney Love, physically assaulting R. Kelly for an action that distressed Jourgensen's daughter, and attacking Metallica with vegetables. He also insisted that Limp Bizkit frontman Fred Durst wear nothing but a cowboy hat during a vocal session he produced, blew up Ministry's tour bus with a large firework purchased from a homeless person, and was ejected from the Grammy Awards for screaming at Beyoncé. "Al Jorgensen stole drugs from Courtney Love. He punched out our kelly for doing something that freaked out his daughter. He attacked Metallica with some vegetables."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Chester Bennington Collaboration
xref.body: Chester Bennington contributed his talents to a side project undertaken by DJ Lethal, who is also known as the DJ for Limp Bizkit. "Chester contributed to a side project by DJ Lethal, Lempiscus DJ."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Contribution to Nu-Metal
xref.body: Despite controversies, Body Count persevered and played a significant role in the emergence of the nu-metal movement during the mid to late 1990s, influencing bands like KoRn, Slipknot, and Limp Bizkit. "But the band continued, and they were a big part of the move into new metal in the middle in late 90s. So basically, you can draw a line from Body Count, right through corn, slipknot, and limp biscuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Nu-Metal Bands
xref.body: Living Color's fusion of funk and metal proved influential, inspiring groups like Rage Against the Machine and Limp Bizkit. "another band that inspired groups like Rage Against the Machine, and Limbiscuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Breakup Member Success
xref.body: After House of Pain broke up, two members achieved further fame independently: Everlast and DJ Lethal, who went on to join Limp Bizkit. "After they broke up, two members would find more fame on their own. There was Everlast, and then there's DJ Lethal, who landed up with Limp Biscuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rock Act Breakthrough
xref.body: Creed was noted as one of the rock acts that managed to break through in a big way around the end of the 1990s, alongside bands like Limp Bizkit and Korn. "And then we had, well, I'll just say it, Creed."
